extracted.intended_audience: general public; readers interested in entertainment, comedy, and cultural controversy
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating stand-up or public-comedy material for cultural sensitivity and acceptability, especially regarding jokes about racial or indigenous groups, and appropriate responses when past material resurfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid racist or demeaning jokes about indigenous people
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that single out Aboriginal/indigenous women (or other racialized groups) as the butt of sexualized or demeaning humor are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics called Noah's comments 'utterly unacceptable' and accused him of 'perpetrating & encouraging racial abuse.' Examples/anti-patterns: describing Aboriginal women in sexualized, stereotyped, or dehumanizing terms ('maybe they'll just like, jump on top of you' with a suggestive gesture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm is judged by impact, not comedic intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if framed as a joke or framed with intent to be humorous, comments that cause offense or perpetuate stereotypes are subject to condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article shows that comedic framing ('All women of every race can be beautiful... Yet.') did not prevent backlash; public figures should recognize that intent does not erase harm. Critics (e.g., Anita Heiss: 'appalled and disgusted') illustrate this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public apology and concrete corrective action when offending
rubrics_metrics.description: When past or present remarks are found offensive, the performer should acknowledge inappropriateness and take steps to mitigate harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trevor Noah admitted the joke was inappropriate, said he 'vowed never to make a joke like that again,' and pledged 'I'll make sure the clip from 2013 is not promoted in any way.' Effective corrective actions include public apology, removing/promoting takedowns, and pledging behavioral change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage directly with affected communities and seek cultural awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists who have caused offense should engage with the communities harmed, offer apologies, and undergo cultural education or dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Joe Williams offered to 'take him to community for some cultural awareness & front and apologise to our staunch and beautifully caring women.' Noah responded he was 'always open to learning more' and willing to visit community — illustrating community engagement as a remediation step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past material can resurface and have present consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Old routines or clips (e.g., a 2013 stand-up bit) can be redistributed and trigger contemporary backlash, including calls for boycotts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2013 clip resurfaced online and Australians called for a boycott of Noah's upcoming tour; performers and promoters should be aware that archival content may harm current reputation and plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove or avoid promoting offensive content from circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking down offensive videos or ensuring clips are not promoted is a recommended immediate response to reduce further harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The video 'has now been taken down' and Noah pledged to 'make sure the clip from 2013 is not promoted in any way.' Platforms, promoters, and performers share responsibility to limit spread of harmful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership in a marginalized group does not excuse harmful remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a person of color or from another marginalized group does not make one immune from perpetuating racial abuse or from valid criticism for such remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joe Williams pointed out: 'As a man of colour, you are usually in point with racism & divide - here you are perpetrating & encouraging racial abuse!!' This highlights that identity does not automatically justify or negate harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public figures should demonstrate sustained behavior change after criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises to stop making certain kinds of jokes should be backed by observable changes (no repeat offenses, educational engagement, changed choices in material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noah said he 'hasn't' made such jokes since learning about Aboriginal history firsthand; demonstrating ongoing change (e.g., visiting communities, altering material) is part of restoring trust.
